w: The summit tops 4,807 m at the France-Italy border, the highest point in Europe outside the Caucasus. Chamonix, at its foot, staged the first Winter Olympics in 1924. The classic Gouter Route to the top takes two days; a cable car crosses the range to Courmayeur via the Col du Geant.
s: Europe's highest peak, 4,807m at the France-Italy border
_facts: 4,807.3m, highest in Europe outside the Caucasus
Chamonix hosted the first Winter Olympics, 1924
Cable car crosses to Courmayeur via Col du Geant
11.6km road tunnel beneath the massif, built 1957-1965

w: At 4,208 m, its highest point, Pointe Walker, was first reached on 30 June 1868 by Horace Walker with guides Melchior Anderegg, Johann Jaun and Julien Grange. The lower Pointe Whymper (4,184 m) had fallen three years earlier, on 24 June 1865, to Edward Whymper's party.
_facts: 4,208m; highest point is Pointe Walker
First climbed 30 June 1868 by Horace Walker with guides Anderegg, Jaun and Grange
Pointe Whymper (4,184m) first climbed 24 June 1865 by Edward Whymper's party

w: At 4,122 m, its French name is usually read as 'Green Needle' - but some scholars trace 'verte' to a pre-Celtic term meaning 'high place', which would make it the High Needle instead. It rises in the Mont Blanc massif above Chamonix, one of the valley's defining aiguilles.
s: The 'Green Needle' that may really mean 'High Needle'
_facts: Name usually translated 'Green Needle'
Possible pre-Celtic root meaning 'high place' instead

w: Two summits rise east of Les Praz: the Grande Aiguille du Dru (3,754 m) and the Petit Dru (3,733 m). The Petit Dru's north face is reckoned one of the six great north faces of the Alps. Its southwest Bonatti Pillar, and the classic route up it, were wiped out by a rockfall in 2005.
s: The shattered needle above Les Praz
_facts: Grande Aiguille du Dru 3,754m; Petit Dru 3,733m
Petit Dru north face: one of the Alps' six great north faces
Bonatti Pillar and its route destroyed by rockfall, 2005

w: The name means 'Cursed Mountain' in French - and until the late 18th century that curse extended to its bigger neighbour too: Mont Blanc and its satellite peaks were collectively known as the Montagne Maudite. It stands 4,465 m high in the massif.
s: The 'Cursed Mountain' on Mont Blanc's shoulder
_facts: Name means 'Cursed Mountain'
Mont Blanc itself was once called part of the 'Montagne Maudite'

w: At 4,001 m, the peak sits on the Rochefort arete between the Dent du Geant and the Grandes Jorasses, usually taken in during a traverse of that ridge rather than climbed alone. James Eccles reached the top with guides Alphonse and Michel Payot on 14 August 1873.
s: First climbed by an Englishman and two Payot guides, 1873
_facts: On the Rochefort arete between Dent du Geant and Grandes Jorasses
First climbed 14 Aug 1873 by James Eccles with guides Alphonse and Michel Payot

w: At 4,000 m it is the lowest of the Alps' 4000-metre summits, but its north face rises 1,600 m from the Argentiere basin at an average angle of 60 degrees, the steepest face on the ridge running from the Aiguille Verte to Mont Dolent. Its dangers later featured on I Shouldn't Be Alive.
s: The lowest 4000er, with the Alps' steepest face
_facts: 4,000m, lowest of the Alps' 4000m peaks
North face: 1,600m at roughly 60 degrees, steepest on the ridge
North face first climbed 1930; featured on I Shouldn't Be Alive

w: Five rock spires over 4,000 m line the Devil's Ridge on Mont Blanc du Tacul, tallest first: L'Isolee, Pointe Carmen, Pointe Mediane, Pointe Chaubert and Corne du Diable. Pointe Carmen fell first, in 1923; the rest followed in 1925, to climbers including Armand Charlet.
s: Five rock needles conquered one by one, 1923-25
_facts: Five needles, all over 4,000m, on the Devil's Ridge of Mont Blanc du Tacul
First needle (Pointe Carmen) climbed 1923; remaining four in 1925
All five climbed in one expedition in 1928 by O'Brien and Underhill with guide Armand Charlet
